decision_question: Does Company C pass the quality screen for inclusion in a long-term India-focused portfolio?

claims.text: The company has a durable competitive position.
The company's financial position is strong.
Management and governance are of good quality.
The company identifies and manages its material sustainability risks.

evidence.text: Company C is the second-largest domestic producer of a key agrochemical intermediate, with a 31 percent share of domestic volumes. It supplies four of the five largest crop-protection companies under multi-year contracts, two of which run to 2031.

The process patent on the main intermediate expires in 2031, after the longest customer contract. The company is backward-integrated into two of its three main raw materials, which management says gives it a cost advantage of 6 to 8 percent over importers.
Revenue was 47.0 billion rupees in FY26, up from 31.5 billion rupees in FY22. EBITDA was 9.0 billion rupees, a margin of 19 percent.

At 31 March 2026 reported borrowings were 12.9 billion rupees and cash and equivalents were 2.1 billion rupees, so reported net debt was 10.8 billion rupees. Reported net debt to EBITDA was 1.2 times, down from 1.9 times a year earlier.

Borrowings falling due within twelve months total 7.4 billion rupees. The company holds 2.1 billion rupees of cash and equivalents and 1.0 billion rupees of undrawn committed credit lines. Management expects to refinance the remainder in the ordinary course.

Note 37. Contingent liabilities not provided for. (a) Income-tax demands under appeal for assessment years 2019 to 2022 amount to 0.6 billion rupees; the company, on legal advice, considers that the demands are unlikely to be sustained. (b) Excise and customs disputes pending before the appellate tribunal amount to 0.3 billion rupees. (c) The company has issued corporate guarantees to the lenders of Greenfield Intermediates Limited, an unconsolidated joint venture in which the company holds 49 percent, with an aggregate outstanding value of 24.0 billion rupees. These guarantees are not included in borrowings and are disclosed in this note only. (d) Claims by former contractors, not acknowledged as debts, amount to 0.2 billion rupees. (e) Letters of credit and bank guarantees issued in the ordinary course of business in favour of customs authorities amount to 0.4 billion rupees. The company does not expect any material outflow in respect of items (a), (b), (d) and (e).

source.title: Annual report FY26: notes to the accounts, note 37

evidence.text: Greenfield Intermediates Limited informed its lenders that it would not meet the instalment due on 30 September 2026. The lenders have agreed a standstill of 90 days. The guarantees given by Company C in respect of the joint venture's borrowings remain in force.
Long-term rating AA-, outlook stable. Last reviewed in March 2026.

evidence.text: Ms Rao joined Company C as chief operating officer in 2019 and became chief executive on 1 April 2023, when the founder moved to the role of non-executive chairman.

source.title: Interview with the chief executive, trade press

evidence.text: Ms Rao has led the company's day-to-day operations since 2019 and has overseen the commissioning of both of its manufacturing plants.

The board has seven directors, four of them independent. The audit committee is chaired by an independent director and met nine times in FY26. The statutory auditor, a large firm in place since 2021, issued an unqualified opinion on the FY26 financial statements.

source.title: Annual report FY26: corporate governance report

evidence.text: Company C reports its scope 1 and 2 emissions and targets a 30 percent cut in emissions intensity by 2030 against a 2022 baseline. It has commissioned an effluent-treatment upgrade at both plants. Water stress at the main plant is identified in the annual report as a material risk.
The company opened a new corporate office in the city in 2024 and employs about 2,300 people.
Company C received an industry award for export performance in 2025.
Capital expenditure in FY26 was 3,100 million rupees, mainly for a new production line at the main plant.
He described Company C as reliable on quality, but said the company appears stretched on working capital. His firm moved about 10 percent of its volumes to a second supplier in 2026.

source.title: Trade interview with a customer's head of procurement
